sections.html:
Hemibarbus mylodon is a cyprinid endemic to the Korean peninsula, where it occurs throughout North Korea and South Korea. A predominantly riverine fish, it lives in clear, well-oxygenated running water over sand, gravel, rock or mud, and adults tend to form schools just above the substrate in faster-flowing sections.

  • Needs a very large tank
  • Needs to be in a group

Endemic to the Korean peninsula where it occurs throughout North Korea and South Korea.

Type locality is 'Keumsan River, near Busan, South Korea.'

Predominantly a riverine fish preferring clear, well-oxygenated, running waters with substrates of sand, gravel, rock or mud, where adults tend to form schools just above the substrate in faster-flowing sections.
Wild fish feed primarily on benthic macroinvertebrates.

Hemibarbus: from the Ancient Greek ἡμι- (hēmi-), meaning 'half', and the generic name Barbus, to which members appear similar.

mylodon: from the Ancient Greek, meaning 'grinder', and ὀδών (odṓn), meaning 'toothed', in allusion to the large fourth pharyngeal tooth, which is molariform with a small, round excavation on the upper surface.

• Berg, L. S. (1907). Review of the freshwater fishes of Korea. Zoologicheskogo Muzeya Imperatorskoj Akademii Nauk v. 12, 1-12
  • Jang, M.-H., M. C. Lucas and G.-J. Joo (2003). The fish fauna of mountain streams in South Korean national parks and its significance to conservation of regional freshwater fish biodiversity. Biological Conservation 114, 115-126
